---
title: "The coefficient of determination"
---

The [least-squares fit](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd) minimizes the sum of squared residuals. The [**coefficient of determination**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) compares that fitted sum with the sum obtained from an intercept-only model.

If we ignored surprisal, we
could assign every word the sample mean log reading time. The coefficient of
determination, written $R^2$, measures the proportional reduction in squared
error obtained by replacing that mean-only prediction with the fitted line.

Thus, $R^2$ compares the fitted line with a mean-only baseline based on the same
observed responses.

## Defining the baseline error

The mean-only prediction for every observation is $\bar y$. Its [**total sum of squares (SST)**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is

$$
\mathrm{SST}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2.
$$

The word *total* refers to observed variation around the sample mean. It does not refer to all variation that could
occur in the population.

For the six constructed log reading times used on the fitting page,

$$
\bar y=5.95.
$$

The first response contributes

$$
(5.78-5.95)^2=.0289
$$

to the baseline error. Adding the six contributions gives

$$
\mathrm{SST}=.0902.
$$

## Defining the fitted-line error

The fitted line assigns observation $i$ the conditional mean
$\widehat y_i$. Its [**sum of squared errors (SSE)**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is

$$
\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.
$$

Since the line was chosen to minimize this quantity, its value cannot exceed the squared error of the
mean-only line. For the six observations,

$$
\mathrm{SSE}\approx.000914.
$$

The fitted line thus leaves much less squared error than the mean-only
prediction. We can express this reduction as

$$
R^2
=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}.
$$

Substituting the two values gives

$$
R^2
=1-\frac{.000914}{.0902}
\approx.9899.
$$

The fitted line reduces observed squared error by about 98.99 percent relative
to predicting the sample mean for every word.

## Verifying the calculation in R

We define the observations again so that the page can be executed on its own.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-r-squared-by-hand
#| echo: true
reading_times <- data.frame(
  surprisal = 2:7,
  log_rt = c(5.78, 5.82, 5.93, 5.99, 6.05, 6.13)
)

fit <- lm(log_rt ~ surprisal, data = reading_times)

sst <- sum((reading_times$log_rt - mean(reading_times$log_rt))^2)
sse <- sum(residuals(fit)^2)
r_squared <- 1 - sse / sst

c(sst = sst, sse = sse, r_squared = r_squared)
summary(fit)$r.squared
```

The two calculations of $R^2$ agree. The first exposes the comparison, while the
second retrieves the value stored by the fitted-model summary.

## Interpreting the baseline precisely

An $R^2$ of $.60$ would mean that the fitted line reduces squared error by 60
percent relative to the observed sample mean. It would not mean that 60 percent
of each reading time has been explained. Nor would it mean that 60 percent of
the causes of reading-time variation have been identified.

That stronger causal reading is not licensed. $R^2$ compares two collections of sample predictions. The comparison
does not identify why the association occurs.

The baseline also matters. If the sample contains only a narrow range of
surprisal values, total variation around the sample mean may be small. The same
amount of residual error can then produce a lower $R^2$ than it would in a
sample with a wider response range. Values from studies with different sampling
designs are thus not automatically comparable.

## Understanding why adding predictors raises sample $R^2$

Suppose we add another predictor to an ordinary least-squares model. The larger
model could assign that new coefficient a value of zero and reproduce every
fitted value from the smaller model. Thus its minimized squared error can stay
the same or decrease, but it cannot increase. Since SST is unchanged,
sample $R^2$ can stay the same or increase.

This mathematical property is not evidence that every added predictor supplies
a useful generalization. It says only that a more flexible model can match the
responses used to fit it at least as well. Later model-comparison pages develop
separate tools for questions about predictions beyond those responses.

## Keeping the claim narrow

A large sample $R^2$ does not establish that the line is straight enough, that
the conditional response variance is constant, that the observations are independent, or
that the predictor has a causal effect. Each claim requires its own evidence.

The constructed data have $R^2\approx.99$ because the six responses were chosen
to lie very close to a line. This makes the arithmetic transparent. It
should not set an expectation for the proportion of reading-time variation that
a single lexical predictor will account for in real data.
